items.prompt: normalizeShoppingState receives { recipeSlugs: ['soup', 'soup', 'missing', 42, null] } against a cookbook whose only recipe is soup. What comes out as recipeSlugs?
items.answer: ['soup']: non-strings, unknown slugs and the repeat are all filtered out
distractors: ['soup', 'soup']: deduplication only applies to slugs that failed validation
[]: mixed types in the array make the guard clause return the empty state
['soup', 'missing']: membership is only checked later, when validKeys is built
items.explanation: Four jobs in one expression: is-array guard, type predicate (drops 42 and null), domain membership against the cookbook (drops 'missing'), then [...new Set(...)] (dedupes) - insertion order preserved, first occurrence wins.

items.prompt: Storage holds { recipeSlugs: 'soup' } - a bare string. The guide contrasts the Array.isArray guard with a bare `[...input.recipeSlugs]`. What would that unguarded spread have produced?
items.answer: ['s', 'o', 'u', 'p'], because a string is iterable and spreads into its characters
distractors: A TypeError, because the spread operator accepts only real arrays, never plain strings
['soup'], because spreading a non-array value wraps it in a one-element array
An empty array, because a primitive string has no elements for the spread to copy
items.explanation: Strings are iterable, so `[...'soup']` gives the string's characters; the guard yields [] instead. (The real code calls `input.recipeSlugs.filter(...)` before any spread, so without the guard a string would actually throw a TypeError at .filter - strings have no filter method; the guide's bare spread is the quieter failure.) input is typed Record<string, unknown> precisely so the compiler will not let you skip the runtime check; JSON and TypeScript know nothing about what the bytes actually contain.

items.prompt: The filter callback is annotated (slug): slug is string. What breaks if you delete that annotation?
items.answer: Compilation: filter returns unknown[], which is not assignable to string[]
distractors: Runtime behavior: without it, the filter would no longer remove the numbers
Nothing: TypeScript infers the narrowing from the typeof comparison alone
Deduplication: the Set would compare unknown values by reference instead
items.explanation: A type predicate is how you tell the compiler a runtime check narrowed the type - the hand-written counterpart of what a schema library's parse() returns. The runtime filtering is identical either way.

items.prompt: A stored document has checked and quantity entries for soup:2, but today's cookbook ships soup with only two ingredients (indexes 0 and 1). What happens on load?
items.answer: The slug survives, but both soup:2 entries are dropped as no longer valid keys
distractors: The whole document is rejected, as one key points past the ingredient count
All entries are kept, as keys are validated by slug prefix rather than index
Only the checked entry is dropped, as quantities are bounded by length, not by key
items.explanation: validKeys is computed from today's ingredient array, not from the stored keys - a schema migration that needs no migration code, pinned by regression test 4.

items.prompt: Instead of removing an ingredient, the cookbook swaps the order of two ingredients in a recipe. What does the normalizer do with a shopper's saved checkmarks and overrides?
items.answer: Nothing, as every slug:index key still exists and intent attaches to the wrong items
distractors: validKeys detects the swap and drops the two shifted entries when the page next loads
The checklist crashes, as two of the overrides now collide on one key
Overrides are re-matched by ingredient name, so only the checkmarks drift
items.explanation: This is the real limit of positional keys: removal heals automatically, reordering corrupts invisibly (the saved intent silently moves). Stable per-ingredient ids would be the fix.

items.prompt: A shopper deliberately blanks the quantity text for an ingredient. Why does the display code use the nullish-coalescing operator rather than logical OR for the fallback?
items.answer: An empty-string override is a real value, and || would bring back the recipe text
distractors: Logical OR cannot be applied to string operands under strict TypeScript settings
Nullish coalescing is faster, as it skips evaluating the fallback
The two operators behave identically here, as a saved override is never empty
items.explanation: '' is falsy but not nullish: it means 'I cleared this'. ingredientsWithQuantities does quantities[key] ?? ingredient.quantity, so only a genuinely absent key falls back to the source recipe.

items.prompt: Storage holds quantities: { 'soup:0': 0 } - a valid key with a number value. Which check removes it, and what would go wrong if it survived?
items.answer: The typeof-string check, as a surviving number would reach code typed for strings
distractors: The key check, as a numeric value makes its key invalid for the recipe
The length bound, as a number has no length property and fails v.length
Nothing does, as zero is coerced to the string '0' when the state is persisted
items.explanation: A naive 'drop keys I do not recognise' keeps this entry - the key IS valid. Only the value type check protects downstream code (rendering and the clipboard formatter) that the compiler already believes is safe; otherwise a runtime type error arrives from storage.

items.prompt: Storage holds checked: { 'soup:0': 'false' } - a string. Why is typeof-boolean the only acceptable check here?
items.answer: 'false' is a truthy string, so a Boolean(v) check would mark the item checked
distractors: JSON stores a boolean as the string 'false', so the value must be parsed first
A truthiness check on the string 'false' would throw instead of coercing
typeof is needed to keep numbers, which are also valid checkmark values
items.explanation: The string 'false' is the trap: any implementation written as if (v) or Boolean(v) inverts the user's intent. The strict type check simply refuses non-booleans.

items.prompt: localStorage.setItem starts throwing (quota exceeded, private mode). What does the shopping list do?
items.answer: It catches the error, stays usable in memory, and sets a storageError flag
distractors: It retries the write with exponential backoff until the quota clears
It rolls the in-memory state back to the last successfully saved snapshot
The exception propagates, so clicks appear to do nothing until a reload
items.explanation: The persist effect catches the error and flips storageError so the UI can disclose that progress is not being saved. The guide's principle: storage failure is disclosed rather than hidden behind a claim that progress was saved. Nothing is lost mid-session; only persistence is at risk.

items.prompt: A shopper pastes a 150-character string into a quantity field and setQuantity runs. What happens?
items.answer: The handler returns early and state is untouched (the same 100-char bound)
distractors: The value is truncated to its first 100 characters, and that is then saved
The value lives in memory for the session but is stripped on the next reload
normalizeShoppingState throws, and the error is surfaced via storageError
items.explanation: setQuantity applies the normalizer's 100-character bound at the input boundary. Validation rejects what the operation cannot accept - and setQuantity then funnels the whole next state back through normalizeShoppingState, so the write path and the load path share one set of rules.

items.prompt: Exercise 1 adds a reset-to-recipe-quantity button. Why must it delete the override key instead of calling setQuantity(key, '')?
items.answer: An absent key falls back to the recipe amount, while '' is itself a saved override
distractors: Empty strings fail the normalizer's length bound and poison the document
setQuantity cannot write empty strings, as the input is required
Deleting the key is only an optimization that keeps the stored JSON document small
items.explanation: Blanking would show no quantity at all after reload. The broken version passes any test that reads the input field and reveals itself only after a round trip, where the nullish-coalescing fallback correctly honours the empty override. Assert the key's absence, not the displayed value.

items.prompt: For the servings-multiplier exercise, what does parseFloat('2 1/2 cups') evaluate to, and what is the consequence for a doubled shopping list?
items.answer: 2: parsing stops at the space, so the doubled list asks for 4 cups, not 5
distractors: 2.5: parseFloat understands mixed-number fractions, so the list says 5 cups
NaN: the trailing unit makes the whole string unparsable as a number
A SyntaxError: parseFloat rejects any non-numeric suffix text in the string
items.explanation: The fraction is silently dropped. That is why the solution parses into a deliberately small grammar and returns null for anything outside it - silent partial parses are wrong exactly where the user cannot verify by eye.

items.front: normalizeShoppingState (src/store/shoppingState.ts:8-25) is called a 'hand-written runtime schema'. Name its four steps and the boundaries where the identical shape recurs.
items.back: Shape guard (reject non-objects), type check (typeof per field), domain check (slug must exist in the cookbook), bound (quantity <= 100 chars). The same four steps guard every trust boundary - localStorage JSON, fetch responses, HTTP request bodies, DB rows - whether written by hand or declared with a schema library like Zod.

items.front: On bad input, this normalizer silently drops the offending entry (src/store/shoppingState.ts:22-23), while a server validator for the same shape rejects the whole request with a 400. Why opposite choices?
items.back: In the browser the untrusted party is the user's own stale storage and there is no caller to inform, so quietly restoring a usable state is kind. On a server, dropping a child record would turn a malformed request into a half-saved one, so the API must refuse and report the issues. Neither policy is universally right; the boundary decides.

items.front: Overrides and checkmarks are keyed slug:index (src/store/shoppingState.ts:15). Ingredient REMOVAL heals automatically on load. Which catalog change corrupts user data without tripping any guard, and what fixes it?
items.back: Reordering ingredients: every positional key still exists, so saved intent silently attaches to the wrong rows. The fix is identity, not validation - stable per-ingredient ids as override keys, so position changes can no longer reassign a shopper's edits.

items.front: The persist effect wraps localStorage.setItem in try/catch and sets a storageError flag on failure (src/store/ShoppingListContext.tsx:46-53). What principle is at work, and what does the naive alternative cost?
items.back: Disclose persistence failure instead of claiming progress was saved: the session keeps working in memory while the UI can warn that changes will not survive a reload. Swallowing the exception instead shows checkmarks that silently vanish on the next visit - a correctness lie, not a crash.
